newsitem.title: GERMANY: German ministries oppose EU majority voting.
newsitem.headline: German ministries oppose EU majority voting.

text.p: While Germany carries the banner of the European Union's drive towards closer integration, some ministries are holding out against giving up their veto on key policy decisions, officials said on Monday.

A number of Bonn government departments oppose introducing so-called qualified majority voting (QMV) -- flying in the face of the line being pushed by pro-Europe Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel ahead of an EU summit in Dublin on Sunday.
Kinkel, writing in Monday's Die Welt newspaper, said the summit would give "a new impulse" to talks on readying the EU for further expansion.
Topping his list of priorities, Kinkel said that majority decisionmaking was needed "as a ground rule in all areas -- including common foreign and security policy.
"Maintaining unanimity while the number of member states grows will lead to stagnation and retreat," Kinkel wrote.

But a spokesman from Kinkel's own ministry said it had not yet replied in writing to a questionnaire on majority voting recently sent out by the Irish government, current holders of the rotating EU presidency.
Too many of German Chancellor Helmut Kohl's ministers, it seems, oppose the idea.
Finance Minister Theo Waigel -- a leading advocate of the European single currency -- said no to majority voting on the question of harmonising tax policy, a spokesman confirmed.
"This is normal. Tax policy is primarily a national matter," he told Reuters, adding that policy harmonisation was being discussed within the framework of ongoing talks.
The interior ministry opposed QMV in security and asylum policy, while the economics ministry did not want rule changes which would expose small firms to cheap foreign competition.

Agriculture Minister Jochen Borchert wants to boost the EU council of ministers' powers to initiate measures at the expense of the Commission, a ministry spokesman said. But the spokesman denied reports Borchert opposed majority voting.
The results of the survey shocked a German commissioner in Brussels, Monika Wulf-Mathies, who told news magazine Der Spiegel Kohl's ministers were "Eurosceptic foot-draggers".

Government sources said they had verbally conveyed the ministries' position ahead of the summit, and deflected charges that the Germans were being bad Europeans by saying that other countries had also shown reluctance to commit fully to QMV.
Ireland is under pressure to speed up negotiations, part of the inter-governmental conference intended to produce a draft treaty in time for a special EU summit in December.
Kinkel flies to Paris on Wednesday for talks with his French counterpart Herve de Charette, and will turn up in Dublin with calls for more flexibillity in an enlarged Union.
Germany's position is mainly aimed at overcoming the delays caused by British foot-dragging.

Bonn wants to prevent a single state from blocking projects agreed on by a big majority of countries. Opponents should not be forced into taking part in projects, but should be given the opportunity to join in later, news weekly Der Spiegel said.
"In a Union of 20 or more members the slowest ship cannot hold up the convoy. The blockade of the union by a single member state must in future be prevented," Kinkel wrote.
